title: System Services: Service Execution
summary: Service Execution is the Windows sub technique in which the Service Control Manager, the process named services.exe, is used to run a payload. The manager is reachable through sc.exe, net.exe, PowerShell service cmdlets, the services console, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) and the service control application programming interface, and all of these can be aimed at a remote host, which makes the technique a favourite for lateral movement. Two shapes appear: an existing service is reconfigured so that its binary path points at adversary code, or a temporary service is created, started and deleted within seconds. Remote execution tooling follows the second pattern, briefly installing a service whose image is a copy of the tool or a launcher. Artefacts are rich, including Security event 4688 for process creation, System event 7045 for a new service, service control manager operational events, registry writes under the services key, and a service image path in a temporary directory. Legitimate administration uses the same tools, so defenders weight the account, the source host, the binary path and the service lifetime.

beginner.definition: This is the Windows version of running code through the service system. The attacker uses tools such as sc.exe to create a service or to change one. The service manager then starts the attacker's program. The action often happens on a remote computer, which helps the attacker spread from machine to machine.
beginner.whyItMatters: Service tools are present on every Windows computer and often work across the network, so this is a common step when an attacker moves between machines. The commands resemble ordinary administration, and a busy support team may not notice them. A service that exists for only a few seconds and runs a file from a temporary folder is a strong warning sign that deserves immediate attention.
howItWorks: The attacker holds an account with administrator rights on the target Windows computer.
They create a new service, or change an existing one, so that its program path points at their payload.
They start the service, and the service control manager runs the payload with high rights.
With common remote tools the service is created, started and deleted again within a few seconds.
The service may also be left in place, so that the payload runs again after every restart.
Defenders check the service name, the program file path and how long the service existed.
beginner.example: Imagine an office building with a plant room that runs the lifts and the lights. A contractor can add a new item to the control panel and switch it on. The panel never asks why. A person who adds an item that powers their own device gets that device running, even inside a locked room. Service execution on Windows works through just such a control panel.
takeaways: New service creation and service start events belong in your alerting, especially on servers.
A service image path in a temporary or user folder is far more suspicious than a normal program path.
Short lived services can still mean remote execution, so keep process and service logs long enough to review.

objectives: Explain how the Windows Service Control Manager is used to execute a payload.
Describe the difference between reconfiguring an existing service and creating a temporary one.
Name the Windows log sources and events that record service creation and process creation.
Explain why remote service tools are useful for moving between computers.
Describe how to judge suspicious service activity against normal administrator behaviour.
